images.caption: Figure 3:Overview of History Forcing. An AR teacher predicts the same noisy student chunk with and without additional history. The resulting history contrast modifies the reference score in DMD and the velocity target in on-policy self-distillation.

Figure 4:Comparison of distillation targets, where++and−-denote distributions with and without additional history.(a) DMDuses a reference close to the data distribution without history.(b) AR Distillationuses the history-conditioned AR distribution, with larger modeling error.(c) History Forcingtransfers the history-induced shift from the AR teacher to the reference, producing a target closer to the data distribution with history.

Figure 5:Qualitative comparisons of consistency.(a)Temporal consistency in 60s autoregressive video generation with Self-Forcing, LongLive, Rolling Forcing, and History Forcing.(b,c)Revisit consistency in video world models, with each pair showing the baseline and History Forcing.

Figure 6:Additional qualitative comparisons of out-of-sight world modeling with the baseline and History Forcing:(a)sand filling,(b)tomatoes into a bowl,(c)coffee pouring, and(d)purple solution pouring.

Figure 7:Additional qualitative comparisons of 15s video generation:(a)a violin performance in a candle-lit chapel,(b)a desert carnival,(c)bread baking,(d)a Tokyo street,(e)a glacial cave, and(f)a Hong Kong tram.
Figure 8:Additional qualitative comparisons of 60s video generation: brushing teeth in front of a mirror.
Figure 9:Additional qualitative examples of 60s video generation with History Forcing:(a)making dumplings,(b)playing an acoustic guitar, and(c)a chef preparing a dish in a kitchen.
